#303. Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger

Modeling predicts plume of neurotoxic lead could reach up to 100 miles away.

In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army announced Thursday that it would delay a plan to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week.

The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week.

“Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday. “Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information.”

Telle claimed that the Army could not delay the detonation any further than Monday due to the state of deterioration of the compound, which is extremely explosive and sensitive. “This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”

Lead azide is a compound used in detonators for munitions and is stockpiled by the US military. In March, the US Army identified that the stockpile in the Iowa facility—the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP)—had deteriorated. The lead azide in the 68 barrels, reported to total around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons), is suspended in a mixture of water and ethanol within the ECMs, but has degraded and crystallized over time. Temperature fluctuations can cause lead azide to dissolve into the water/alcohol solution and recrystallize into needles or platelets, the Army said. In crystallized forms, lead azide becomes extremely sensitive to any physical shock, friction, or heat. The Army determined the current state is a “catastrophically hazardous condition.”

In an environmental assessment released Wednesday, the Army said that trying to move the lead azide from its current position for any reason was ruled out. Any sloshing or physical shock from loading, transporting, or burying the barrels for safer detonation would create “an unacceptable safety risk and a high probability of accidental, uncontrolled detonation.”

The military considered neutralizing the lead azide using a chemical reagent, but again ruled it out because it said the process would require handling the lead azide over an extended period, with barrels neutralized at a rate of 3 to 10 per day. “The chemical neutralization process requires significantly more ‘hands-on’ time and physical manipulation of the drums by personnel over a prolonged 7- to 22-day period, drastically increasing the probability of accidental, fatal detonation during handling,” the Army wrote in its assessment.

In all, the Army considered a controlled, mitigated “Blow-in-Place” plan the best option, and it specifically planned for a fall detonation. The Army said the fall weather would “take advantage of periods of reduced thermal cycling and to ensure the lowest impact to facility operations and local agriculture (harvesting).”

According to an emergency permit for the detonation from the Environmental Protection Agency, the plan is to place explosive charges and an accelerant on or near each of the ECMs.

The Army intends to try to mitigate the detonation’s impact with a few simple methods. Those include lime-fill and sand-fill barriers around the ECMs, water cannons and misters to control lead dust in the wake of the explosion, and timing the detonation with ideal weather conditions—avoiding high winds that could increase the area exposed to the plume or, conversely, a thermal inversion that could trap the plume in one place.

Modeling released Wednesday—based on the conditions for the scheduled detonation on Friday—suggested the plume could deposit lead dust at an amount between 5 and 100 micrograms per square foot in a stretch up to 25 miles north, nearly to Wapello, Iowa. Those levels are above those considered hazardous for floors and windows, respectively. Meanwhile, airborne lead, at a level of 0.18 micrograms per cubic meter, would reach nearly 100 miles north, toward Cedar Rapids, Iowa. The EPA standard for lead levels in the air is 0.15 micrograms per cubic meter.

During the detonation, the Army advised residents in the immediate area to consider leaving or at least staying indoors with windows closed.  It also recommended people wash their cars if they park outside. Similarly, local fire departments reportedly planned to hose down children’s playgrounds to remove any coating of lead dust in the aftermath, and schools planned closures.

The Army’s plan was to communicate clearly with the public about the plans, including holding an open-house event on October 15. But while Middletown residents may have been aware of the detonations, Iowans in the projected path of the plume were surprised by the news this week.

In its environmental risk assessment, the Army said it planned to mitigate the lead fallout with “rapid excavation” of soil and dust and treat it with a “stabilization agent.” This was to prevent it from remaining in the environment of the military facility, from which it could drift or make its way into groundwater. But the efforts would not mitigate the airborne plume, and lead does not break down in the environment. Children and pregnant people are particularly vulnerable to the neurotoxic effects.

Amid health and environmental fears, state leaders and residents raised a range of questions Wednesday and Thursday, from how the lead azide was allowed to deteriorate to its current hazardous condition and whether the Army had truly exhausted safer options—options that wouldn’t launch a toxic cloud over a swath of the state.

Iowa’s governor-elect, Rob Sand, wrote on social media that an “unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation.”

Political leaders in nearby Illinois also chimed in, sending a letter to Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, expressing “grave concerns” over the plan.

“Alongside our neighbors in Iowa, we are also demanding answers about how this could affect our people’s health and safety,” Illinois Governor JB Pritzker wrote on social media.

On Thursday, prior to the announcement of a delay, environmental groups filed a lawsuit seeking a court-ordered pause of the detonation. The groups alleged, in part, that the EPA approved the plan “without full consideration of less dangerous alternatives that would avoid widespread dispersal and deposition of toxic lead; and inadequate public notice of the plan to open-detonate hazardous waste due to the extraordinarily rushed timeline set by the Army.” Late Thursday, a federal appeals court issued an emergency stay of the Army’s EPA permit for the demolition, halting plans until it can review the case.

Friday morning, the Army, Department of Health and Human Services, and EPA released a joint statement saying:

The entire interagency is working together to ensure that the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa is conducted in the safest fashion possible. Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized. The entire Trump administration will continue to engage with state and local officials, as well as the broader community, to keep all apprised of updates as they arise.

Notably, in June, Zeldin listed the EPA’s work with Iowa’s lead azide as one of the top “100 environmental victories that showcase EPA’s unwavering dedication to protecting American families.” The work was number 60 on the list, described as providing “critical emergency support to Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, deploying technical experts for 68 deteriorating drums of explosive lead azide.”

This post was updated November 20 to include that the federal appeals court granted a stay in the case brought by the environmental groups.

#302. This built-in windows tool can tell if your DirectX has a problem

DxDiag is a handy and free resource for troubleshooting DirectX.

DirectX is Microsoft's proprietary set of programming tools that help computer applications, especially games, communicate with your graphics card, audio and input devices. It allows software and hardware to work together to render graphics, play sound and deliver interactive multimedia experiences. If an application requires a DirectX capability but your computer doesn't support it, the application may fail to launch or crash mid-operation. Identifying the exact source behind these problems can be tricky, as outdated DirectX software, corrupt video card drivers or faulty Windows configuration could be contributing factors. This is where Microsoft's built-in DirectX diagnostic tool (DxDiag) can prove helpful.

DxDiag is a windows utility that scans your computer, collects technical system information and reports on installed DirectX components and drivers. The tool can be used as a convenient starting point to investigate graphics or audio-related issues. It can also generate a condensed text report that you can share with technical support persons for analysis. Understanding the capabilities and limitations of DxDiag can help you make informed decisions when troubleshooting sound, visual or application compatibility issues.

To run the built-in DirectX diagnostic tool, initiate the run command with the windows + R shortcut, then type "dxdiag" and press enter. You can also search for "dxdiag" in the Windows start menu and launch the utility from there. The DxDiag tool includes tabs for System, Display, Sound and Input. It is recommended to tick the "Check for WHQL digital signatures" checkbox to verify the integrity of installed drivers.

The System page includes details on your PC's motherboard, processor, memory and graphics card. It also displays the DirectX version installed on your computer. Meanwhile, the Display page offers a detailed overview of your graphics card, from driver version to supported DirectX features like Direct3D Acceleration and DirectX 12 Ultimate. Similarly, the Sound page includes information on connected audio devices and their driver details, while the Input page lists all IO devices, including your keyboard, mouse and other peripherals. Make sure to review the Notes section at the bottom of Display, Sound and Input pages, since it may list errors reported by DxDiag.

Can DxDiag tell if the DirectX on your computer is corrupted? While it can help identify issues with display, sound and input devices, DxDiag cannot conclusively determine or repair DirectX problems. Just because the utility displays a clean report, it doesn't necessarily rule out all hardware and game-specific issues that your computer might be experiencing.

If DxDiag reports display, sound or IO errors, start by comparing the affected component's driver version to the latest driver available. In case of discrepancy, consider downloading and installing the latest driver from the manufacturer's official website. While Windows update often include driver updates, they are not always guaranteed be up to date. This could potentially result in outdated or incompatible drivers causing game-specific issues even when your hardware meets the recommended system requirements. In case of audio-specific issues, in addition to drivers, also consider verifying that you're using the correct playback device in the Windows sound panel. You may also want check if the affected application or game has a new update or patch addressing hardware-related bugs.

If none of these steps end up resolving your problem, you can try running the sfc /scannow command as a administrator to scan and repair system files. If errors persist even after following these troubleshooting steps, it's recommended to contact Microsoft support and share your DxDiag report to help them investigate graphics, audio or other compatibility issues in your PC.

They're insanely fluffy yet dry faster than you expect."

Whiskey drinkers have specific tastes. Unless you know exactly what they want, then let Flaviar’s 2026 advent calendar do the choosing. This year’s edition hosts 24 great-tasting whiskies from around the globe. Each box comes with guided stories, tasting notes, and digital content for every reveal. Pricewise, it costs less than many Pappy Van Winkle releases.

For the right kind of dad (or a very cool mom), it's a gift he'll really appreciate — just be sure to give it to him at Thanksgiving so he has time to savor each day's release.

There's a non-zero chance that your parents, like so many other homeowners with a little disposable income, have procured a 12-foot skeleton from the Home Depot within the last few years. (It can talk now, in case you didn't hear.) If that's the case, this custom Santa costume will give them an excuse to leave it up through the holidays. We won't tell their HOA if you won't.

Apple’s flagship headphones have never been cheap, but thanks to Black Friday sales, the holiday shopping season is your chance to score a pair at a discount — or hope someone especially generous puts them under the tree. This time of year, they're often marked down as low as $449.

Beyond the price, the Apple AirPods Max 2 are an upgrade from the original, boasting the H2 chipset for enhanced active noise cancellation and integrated smart audio features such as Adaptive Audio and Conversational Awareness. They also support true lossless audio over USB-C connection to hear more detail and nuance from Apple Music tracks. Read our full review of the Apple AirPods Max 2.

The travel-friendly Anker Prime Power Bank packs enough power to charge an entire laptop on the go, and it's an incredibly practical gift for anyone with a lot of devices to keep charged (i.e. everyone). Wherever you are, this portable power bank can charge a laptop, a handheld gaming console, and a smartphone — all at the same time.

DJI is best known for its drones, but don't sleep on its creator-friendly cameras and microphones, either. The DJI Mic Mini has a cult following among TikTokkers, and it's a personal favorite of our own reporters. Compatible with both iPhones and Androids (plus a host of cameras), these are the exact microphones that the Mashable social team uses at events such as VidCon. Read our full review of the DJI Mic Mini.

The Mashable Choice Award-winning Insta360 Luna Ultra is a new 8K gimbal camera with dual lenses and a detachable two-inch touchscreen for remote operation. Mashable assistant editor Amanda Yeo thought the latter was a really neat feature: It "turns the Luna Ultra from a nifty handheld camera into a super flexible vlogging tool that can capture more angles with ease, and is particularly attractive for solo shooting," she wrote. It's a solid investment for any aspiring or professional creator. Read our full review of the Insta360 Luna Ultra.

The Octobuddy is a colorful silicone suction mount that lets you stick your phone onto any smooth surface for impromptu videos. TikTok-obsessed teens will undoubtedly appreciate its simple design that makes filming GRWM videos and dance challenges way easier. We frequently see the Octobuddy mentioned in our In My Bag creator interview series.

The latest installment in the Grand Theft Auto series has been 13 years in the making, and we're not being dramatic when we say it's the most anticipated video game of all time. Its story will follow a criminal couple through the streets and swamps of Leonida, a fictional version of Florida. If its soundtrack is anything to go by, it'll be a banger. If you preorder GTA 6 before launch day on Nov. 19, your giftee will get bonus vehicle, weapon, and character cosmetics.

The secret ingredient to some of the very best gifts of 2026? Pure, unadulterated nostalgia.

For its latest remake, Nintendo modernized 1998's Ocarina of Time with better visuals and physics, new voice lines, a fresh score, and free camera controls. According to Mashable tech reporter Alex Perry, who got to play the game for an hour at a press preview event, it's a thoughtful update of a stone-cold classic. "It isn't the same as a brand new Zelda for [the Nintendo] Switch 2," he wrote, "but it'll do until the time comes." It's out Nov. 5, and you can preorder it now.

Clips of Pokopia gameplay went massively viral this spring, and for good reason. It's "Pokémon meets Minecraft, with a delightfully goofy premise and the potential for lots of town-building fun to be had either by yourself or with a group of friends via online play," Perry wrote. It's such a good game that a lot of people upgraded to the Nintendo Switch 2 just to play it. Read Mashable's full review of Pokémon Pokopia.

Perry called the Nintendo Switch 2 "a fabulous follow-up to an all-time legend." It won a Mashable Choice Award for its upgraded system software and great online social features. Perry also loved its new magnetic Joy-Con 2s, which are bigger and more satisfying to use than the original Switch's controllers. We think it's the best handheld gaming console to buy in 2026, even after a price hike. Read our full review of the Nintendo Switch 2.

Lego had retro gamers tweaking last year with its awesome Game Boy replica. For its encore, the iconic toy maker jumped a few gaming generations ahead, creating this Sony PlayStation set in celebration of the system’s 30th anniversary. It’s an awesome recreation of the original and features customizable details paying homage to two classic launch titles: Ape Escape and Gran Turismo. One look is enough to bring back 32-bit-era memories.

For gamers who are spending the entire winter playing GTA 6 in an old, out-of-date wireless headset, we have an upgrade option for you. The new Sony Inzone H9 II Wireless Noise-Cancelling Gaming Headset works for consoles and PC gamers, and it has the same incredible drivers as the new Sony XM6 ANC headphones.

The sixth installment in Sarah J. Maas' hit romantasy series, A Court of Thorns and Roses, arrived this October, and no self-respecting BookTok member should miss it. If you really want to earn brownie points with your bibliophilic giftee, preorder them a copy of the next book, which is set for release in January. Both are available in hardcover, paperback, audiobook, and Kindle e-book formats.

Amazon redesigned its Kindle e-readers for 2026 with fun new colors (ube! seaglass green!) and thinner, lighter form factors. After testing the updated base model, Mashable's Mangino crowned it the best budget e-reader. "What truly makes it stand out is just how lightweight it is," she wrote — at six inches and half a pound, it's excellent for travel. Read our full review of the new Amazon Kindle.

However, if you have a little more wiggle room in your gifting budget, Mangino thinks the new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best Kindle overall: It's waterproof, longer-lasting, and equipped with an adjustable warm light. Read our full review of the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition.

Psst: Don't forget to remove the Kindle lockscreen ads before you gift. To quote our tech editor, "it's borderline rude" not to.

Amazon's first page turner, the Kindle Click, "will level up your cozy evenings spent reading," said Mangino, and it's a must-have for the BookTok set. It lets you turn the pages of a Kindle or adjust its brightness when you're snug under the covers of your fuzziest blanket. (It's compatible with models from 2024 onward.) Unlike other page-turners we've tried, it works via Bluetooth. Read our full review of the Amazon Kindle Click.

A gooseneck stand is a "luxury" for any regular e-reader user because it situates the device "within reading distance without any arm fatigue," Mangino said. Based on her testing, this Magipea model works nicely with both Kindle and Kobo models. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Trivia night at the local bar is fun, but hosting one at home can be even better. Hitster is an icebreaker that gets everyone working together to identify hit songs from the past century. Scan a card to play a track, then guess the year it was released. Themed editions — including All American, Guilty Pleasures, and Latino —broaden playability and let you tailor the music to your company.

Multiple Mashable editors and writers swear by Loop's earplugs, which look like jewelry, fit comfortably in most people's ears, and make a unique stocking stuffer. The Loop Experience 2 are great for regular concert- and music festival-goers; Mashable's Henschel even wore them to a Beyoncé show. "I could hear Beyoncé and her band perfectly, but the din of the stadium was almost completely suppressed," she wrote. They come in a range of color options, including some limited-edition metallic variants designed in partnership with Harry Styles.

This spring, Sony launched some new Bluetooth record players for the first time in seven years. Henschel tried the entry-level PS-LX3BT model and called it "a stylish turntable with idiot-proof plug-and-play functionality." She pointed out that it has a USB-B port in the back, which you can use to rip vinyl tracks onto a laptop. If your partner collects vinyl, this is one of those Christmas gift ideas they'll appreciate for years to come. Read our full review of the Sony PS-LX3BT.

CDs are the latest retro tech to have a resurgence among Gen Z. Tracking down a cool old CD player on eBay will earn you a lot of cred, but if you don't want to go through the trouble, this see-through model from Retradisc looks really, really cool. It works with wired or wireless headphones, and best of all, it doesn't cost as much as Sony's new gold-plated Walkman.

Technics continues to make a strong impression in the wireless audio market. When it comes to hi-fi headphones, the new EAH-A1000 are a sonic stunner that put many category leaders to shame. They crush the AirPods Max 2 in most areas and rival the Sony WH-1000XM6 sound quality, while also outlasting both competitors in playtime (up to 45 hours per charge) and multi-point pairing. Plus, the elegant craftsmanship is a 10/10. Every audiophile should have this at the top of their wish list this year.

Sonos has long been a go-to for WiFi speakers, but JBL’s new Cove Series is a true competitor that offers a compelling wireless audio experience at a more attainable price. If you have someone on your shopping list who loves music, the Cove speaker will fill up their bedroom, living room, or back patio with big sound.

Plus, it even offers automatic self-tuning, AI Sound Boost technology that optimizes audio for listening environments, and hands-free Alexa voice control.

Choosing a signature scent for your hubby isn’t as easy as picking out a video game; you need to know their olfactory preferences. If you’re unsure what they like — or shopping for someone especially particular — let them decide with one of Fulton & Roark’s discovery sets. The variety gives them a chance to explore different scents and narrow down their next go-to fragrance. (Pro tip: We like Palmetto and Ghost Trees.)

Harry’s has something for every man’s mug. Guys who prefer a clean-shaven look can reach for the brand’s shaving kit, which includes the popular Truman handle with secure grip and multiple five-blade cartridges that deliver close shaves. No-shave November devotees can keep their mane well-kempt with the beard wash and conditioning spray bundle.

Every well-groomed gentleman deserves a luxury electric shaver in his life. The Panasonic Arc5 Pro is our pick for its comfortable, close shaves and flexible head, which is designed to improve cutting performance. It works for both wet and dry shaving, and the built-in pop-up trimmer provides seamless control and navigation to clean up edges around the neckline.

We think the Mashable Choice Award-winning Shark CryoGlow is the best red light mask you can buy right now (and one of the best Christmas gifts for women). It provides more complete coverage than other masks from brands like OmniLux or CurrentBody, and each bulb can emit red, blue, or near-infrared light.

Former senior shopping reporter Leah Stodart was convinced that the CryoGlow’s bacteria-killing blue light setting is what finally cleared a year’s worth of her relentless adult acne. Some cooling under-eye pads complete this luxurious self-care device. Read our full review of the Shark CryoGlow.

Several Mashable staffers use Shark's FlexStyle multi-styler on a regular basis. (Mangino did her wedding hair with it!) It costs half as much as Dyson's iconic Airwrap but works just as well, if not better. It supports a ton of different attachments and has a unique twisting base that functions like a regular hair dryer on its own. Read our full review of the Shark FlexStyle.

Routine can give children structure and help them feel more secure. The Skylight Buddy guides kids through mornings, afternoons, and bedtime, while helping them develop healthy habits and independence. They can add and check off chores, events, and tasks. This digital calendar also functions as an alarm clock and nightlight, signaling wake-up and sleep times. Personalization features help families reinforce goals and daily commitments.

The Playground is a cubic gaming console designed for playing family-friendly games with motion controls — no need for a traditional gamepad. Perry described it as "a spiritual successor to the old Xbox Kinect." If this is the first time you're hearing of it, get with the program: It managed to outsell the PlayStation 5 on Black Friday 2025, and was difficult to find in stock during the holiday season last year. If you plan on gifting it within the coming weeks, we'd recommend adding it to your cart ASAP.

Since the viral NeeDoh toys are sold out everywhere, again, we have another viral children's toy that's selling out fast. Kids are obsessed with the colorful and addictive Clickeez keyboard, and you can still find them in stock if you hurry (Amazon is backordered until after Christmas, but Walmart has them).

Like wired earbuds, CD players, and other items from your childhood, Pokémon cards are so incredibly back — and dare we say, bigger than ever. The Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration Elite Trainer Box is a giftable bundle that includes 9 booster packs and plenty of other goodies. Amazon is also selling it on an invite-only basis; try your luck because it's well under market price, as of this writing.

Do you want to inspire a love of music in your kids? The Fender x Loog electric guitar has been reimagined for little hands. The 3-string design is also more kid-friendly, and it comes with chord flashcards so kids can learn to shred. If you've always wanted to have the coolest kid, niece, or nephew on the block, then now you know what to get them for Christmas.

We recently named the Toniebox 2 one of Mashable's Gifts of the Year in our guide to the top gifts for kids. The kid-famous Toniebox is a favorite of the moms and dads on the Mashable team. Whether you're shopping for your own child or trying to earn a reputation as the cool aunt or uncle, kids and parents alike love these screen-free storytelling devices.

If your tyke already has a Toniebox, they can always use more Tonies — the little figures you put on top of the device to activate a new storytime. Bluey and Pokémon Tonies joined the party this year.

Another Mashable Gift of the Year winner, this portable screen-free audio player is a hit with the three kiddos of Nicole Cammorata, Mashable's director of special projects. "Compatible cards power up everything from chapter books and shorter stories to music and learning-based content," she wrote. For an incredibly sweet personalized gift, you can have grandparents, siblings, or friends record custom audio messages on blank Yoto cards.

Don't overthink (or overspend) trying to think of the perfect Christmas gifts for kids. Keep it simple and combine two things kids love — Bluey and slime. This slimy sand adds a bit more texture to the average slime, letting kids mold it in new ways. Even better, you can pick it up for under $15, and still have the best gift under the tree.

Gifting a pair of the best Beats headphones is a sure bet for any fashion-forward music lover. Fans of over-ear headphones will appreciate the modular Beats 360, which features a customizable design with swappable ear cushions, IPX4 sweat resistance, pleasant sound, and strong ANC. True wireless conformists can utilize the sporty Powerbeats Pro 2 for exercise and leisure; the revamped earhook design is optimized for comfort and sound performance.

Looking for the best gifts under $100? The Camp Snap 2 is one of our top picks. This screenless digital camera has six built-in filters and super simple controls. To transfer its photos to your phone, all you need is a USB-C cable. Mangino brought a Camp Snap 2 on her Grecian honeymoon this past summer, "and now I have the sweetest photos to look back on," she said. Read our full review of the Camp Snap 2.

Pimple patches are the kind of genius idea we wish was available when we were teenagers. They turn breakouts into a fashion moment. We can also recommend Peace Out's Pore Perfecting scrub stick. Both of these spot treatments will make great stocking stuffers for teens.

The merchandising gods are working their magic this holiday season in anticipation of the biggest MCU film yet: Avengers: Doomsday. Funko Pop has a tempting lineup of Marvel collectibles, including multiple versions of Doctor Doom, beloved X-Men characters, and a 10-inch jumbo Sentinel. Steve Rogers, Thor, Shang-Chi, and several other familiar faces round out the collection.

If your teenager is allowed to watch TV in their room, upgrade their older set to the Mashable Choice Award-winning Hisense DécoTV. The 32-inch model "is compact enough to fit just about anywhere and simplistically chic enough to fit in with just about any decor," said Stodart. It'll be perfect for their college dorm room when the time comes. As a bonus, it costs much less than Samsung's smallest The Frame TV. Read our full review of the Hisense DécoTV.

No one's too old for Play-Doh anymore: This summer, the modeling clay brand released its first-ever collection of adult craft kits, Blooms by Play-Doh. Each one comes with colorful, scented Play-Doh sticks that they can press and shape into a pretty floral bouquet, plus finishing spray and a clear vase. For crafty types who have grown bored of Lego's Botanical builds, this is one of our favorite Christmas gift ideas.

The new Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8 is the best flip phone we've tested this year, and Mashable's Werth especially recommends it "for a stylish, on-trend young person." It's easy to hold in one hand, durable, and available in an extremely cute purpley-pink color. And while its camera setup isn't wildly impressive, it does take a mean selfie. Read our full review of the Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8.

Retro tech is having another moment. Last year, cassette players were everywhere; this year, Bluetooth CD players are joining the old-school wave (there are two in this gift guide). They’re a fun pick for Gen Alpha teens who love iPods, disposable cameras, and DVDs, and you can pair it with their favorite artists' latest albums.

The Fosi Audio Merak works as a portable and desktop CD player, with modern extras including Bluetooth, USB drive playback, and one-touch CD ripping.

The best Christmas gift for a hostess with the mostest is a Ninja Slushi Twist. It makes delicious frozen cocktails, slushies, and milkshakes just as well as the original Ninja Slushi, but now it works faster, picks settings for you, and adds a second mixing canister. That's right: Two flavors at once, baby. It's "just plain fun, and will make your home the go-to for your friend group," said Stodart, who gave it a Mashable Choice Award. Read our full review of the Ninja SLUSHi Twist.

Bless the tea sipper in your family with this flavorful collection of 18 premium blends that bring winter warmth and wellness. These loose-leaf teas come in plant-based sachets and are sourced from small-scale farmers. The assortment includes multiple varieties of black, green, mint, oolong, and white teas.

The viral Ninja Crispi and the new Cosori Iconic have both earned the Mashable staff's collective seal of approval. Why those air fryers, you might ask? Not only do they crisp up food nicely, but they're free of plastics and forever chemicals. The compact Crispi is ideal for cooking single-serve meals and meal-prepping; its glass containers come with lids for storing your leftovers. The Cosori is a sleeker stainless steel model with a bigger basket and handy smart controls. Read our full review of the Cosori Iconic.

A digital dosing cup with a precision scale for weighing beans before grinding is the gift every coffee drinker didn’t think they needed until now. The Subminimal Subscale powers on quickly and features a hidden LED display for easy-to-read measurements. It can handle hot and cold liquids, and its minimalist design complements modern kitchen counters.

The new Series 12 is the best smartwatch for most iPhone users, in our opinion. It has a faster processor, pretty new ceramic finish options, and an improved heart sensor array. Mashable senior editor Stan Schroeder has been testing it this fall, and he said the latter is "the star of the show" because it "allows for far more frequent measurements." It also "opens the door for new apps such as Readiness and an overhauled Vitals app," he added.

We loved the Google Fitbit Air when we first tested it, and love it even more after the latest update, which supports automatic detection for up to 100 sports and tracks blood pressure trends. It excels as both a fitness tracker and sleep tracker, making it a superb gift that athletes won’t ever take off. Not to mention it’s way more affordable than the Apple Watch Series 12, Oura Ring 5, and Whoop MG. Read our full review of the Fitbit Air.

Almost everyone on Mashable's shopping team owns an Owala FreeSip, which Mangino dubbed the "best water bottle ever." The 24-ounce insulated stainless steel bottle is designed to accommodate both sipping (via straw) and good ol' fashioned gulp when tipped back. For athletes, college students, teenagers, or anyone who drinks water, we think a colorful Owala is one of the best Christmas gifts under $50. Read our full review of the Owala FreeSip.

Mashable tech reporter Matt Binder, a self-proclaimed "longtime soccer dad," tested the new XbotGo Falcon sports tracking camera for an entire youth soccer season this year. His verdict: It's "a smart pick for parents and coaches." Its footage is sharp, you can monitor it in real time from your smartphone, and it works with nine different sports (soon to be 12). It's a bit of a splurge, but unlike a lot of the competition, it doesn't require a subscription. Read our full review of the XbotGo Falcon.

Tossing the football is a holiday tradition for many sports-loving households. This year, rifle this waterproof football into your dad’s chest. Dime Labs cleverly designed its footballs with silicone grip strips for better handling, and a woven microfiber cover to survive the wettest conditions. It comes in two sizes – 10.5 inches and 8.5 inches – with the smaller version well-suited to kids practicing their quarterback skills.

It's a cooler. It's a boombox. It's both! We love the Igloo KoolTunes for its old-school design and surprisingly good audio quality. While it lacks deep bass, it offers clear, balanced sound and can get quite loud. "It's not a gimmick, but a fun fusion of summer party gear," said Mashable's Henschel. Read our full review of the Igloo KoolTunes.

If your favorite man is always lugging around beach chairs and heavy coolers, then give him the gift of free hands and cold drinks this Christmas. The Yeti Hopper M Series Backpack Cooler is discounted right now as part of Amazon's Black Friday sale, so you can even grab it on sale.

The new Shark ChillPill is another Mashable Gift of the Year winner. It's a powerful portable fan that stands out for its swappable misting and cooling plate attachments, long battery life, and fun colorways. (Justin Bieber's SKYLRK brand teamed up with Shark for a limited-edition "Heat" variant, which is long sold out.) It came in clutch for Mangino on some of the hottest days of the summer. Read our full review of the Shark ChillPill.

The LifeStraw is a Black Friday classic that always goes on sale around the holidays, which also makes it a perfect stocking stuffer for people who love camping and the great outdoors. You can stick one end of this straw into virtually any water source — no matter how gross — and clean, filtered water comes out the other end.

Portable Bluetooth speakers are crowd-pleasing gifts for just about anyone, from teenagers to parents, siblings, and friends. This year, we're loving the all-new Tribit StormBox Micro 3. It produces satisfying sound in a compact design, is fully waterproof, and comes in multiple standout colorways. Tribit’s speaker is travel-friendly, with a magnetic snap that can latch onto fridge doors or bike handles.

Simply put, Yeti's stainless steel Rambler tumblers are crowd-pleasers. They're dishwasher-safe, incredibly durable, condensation-resistant, and available in a huge rainbow of colors and patterns. Pro tip: For a very affordable personalized Christmas gift, you can customize a Rambler with your own text, graphics, and logos on the Yeti website.

Power stations can come in handy in lots of unexpected situations. From camping at music festivals to charging up your phone in an emergency blackout, these lightweight and portable devices keep you on the grid. Bluetti makes some of our favorite power stations, and the Elite 30 V2 is a good starter model.

The AirFly Pro is a cult-favorite Bluetooth adapter that makes seatback screens on older planes compatible with wireless headphones. After using it on round-trip flights between Chicago and London, Henschel said she'd "never fly without it again." The newer AirFly Pro 2 has simpler controls, improved sound quality, and pairs faster. Read our full review of the Twelve South AirFly Pro.

Traveling abroad this winter? Take this handy adapter along. Anker’s latest travel charger works with outlets in nearly every country and can charge up to four devices at once. The voltage detection system monitors voltage, power output, and temperature in real time. All readings and charging statuses are displayed on the LCD screen.

Travel jewelry cases are both thoughtful and practical, and we like this one in particular. The velvet box comes in a few different colors, and it ensures your wife, girlfriend, or daughter's favorite rings, necklaces, and earrings never get misplaced when she's away from home. If you're hunting for one of the best Christmas gifts for women under $25, look no further.

Cushy ANC headphones are a non-negotiable for long travel days, and lead shopping reporter Bethany Allard thinks the latest Bose QuietComforts are the best mid-range option for flying. When she wore them on a plane, "I heard minimal engine hum and was able to completely tune out conversations from my fellow passengers," she wrote. "I also never felt the need to remove the headphones due to wear fatigue." Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort headphones (2nd Gen).

Nori’s garment steamers are a lifesaver for business travelers and fashion professionals. The Cloud Max makes de-wrinkling clothes a breeze, using gentle vacuum suction to pull fabric taut for smoother results. Anti-spit technology prevents leaks and water spots, and the steamer’s portable design fits comfortably in any travel bag.

A weekender bag bridges the gap between a backpack and a suitcase. It should hold a few outfits, toiletries, and an extra pair of shoes for a two- or three-day trip. Quince’s Voyage bag fits the bill with a dedicated shoe compartment, multiple pockets, and a padded shoulder strap. It’s currently on sale for half of its original price, while supplies last.

The best Christmas gifts for teenage girls

We recommend sending or ordering your Christmas gifts as soon as you can, as delays can (and will) happen. USPS, FedEx, and UPS will all be delivering on Thursday, Dec. 24 (aka Christmas Eve), but that doesn't guarantee your order will make it off the trucks in time. For Amazon Prime members, check the estimated delivery times on items' product and checkout pages.

FedEx Ground: Dec. 17 to 23 (five to one-day transit, respectively)

If you're looking to save money, then we recommend saving all of your Christmas gift purchases for big sales like Black Friday and Cyber Monday 2026. This year, they fall on Nov. 27 and Nov. 30, respectively, though major retailers like Amazon, Walmart, and Target typically start their holiday sales well ahead of time.

Haley Henschel is a Chicago-based Senior Shopping Reporter at Mashable who reviews and finds deals on popular tech, from laptops to gaming consoles and VPNs. She has years of experience covering shopping holidays and can tell you what’s actually worth buying on Black Friday and Amazon Prime Day. Her work has also explored the driving forces behind digital trends within the shopping sphere, from dupes to 12-foot skeletons.

Timothy Beck Werth is the Tech Editor at Mashable, where he leads coverage and assignments for the Tech and Shopping verticals. Tim has over 15 years of experience as a journalist and editor, and he has particular experience covering and testing consumer technology, smart home gadgets, and men’s grooming and style products. Previously, he was the Managing Editor and then Site Director of SPY.com, a men's product review and lifestyle website. As a writer for GQ, he covered everything from bull-riding competitions to the best Legos for adults, and he’s also contributed to publications such as The Daily Beast, Gear Patrol, and The Awl.

Tim studied print journalism at the University of Southern California. He currently splits his time between Brooklyn, NY and Charleston, SC. He's currently working on his second novel, a science-fiction book.

Alex Bracetti is a freelance product reviewer and journalist covering gadgets and men's grooming products. An experienced consumer tech writer, he has bylines at Mashable, Complex, SPY.com, Thrillist, AskMen, CNN Underscored, and Tom's Guide. In addition to writing about the latest tech trends and gadgets, he's also covered men's fashion, sports, and gaming. For Mashable, he primarily covers headphones/wireless earbuds, party speakers, smartphones, and mobile accessories.

#300. iPad Air vs. iPad Pro: The features you're actually paying $450 extra for

The iPad Pro is Apple's best tablet, but not everyone needs its power.

When choosing your next iPad, it's not a difficult decision if you know the base model works for your needs, or if you want a small tablet. But it's trickier to decide between the iPad Air and iPad Pro if you're using an iPad for work or creative pursuits. Is saving $450 and opting for the still-capable iPad Air something you'll regret in the future?

The iPad Air starts at $749 for the 11-inch model with 128GB of storage and an M4 processor, while the 11-inch M5 256GB base iPad Pro costs $1,199. Both devices offer 13-inch variants if you want a larger screen. Those prices might seem higher than you remember, due to the ongoing RAM crisis that's been spiking consumer tech prices. Apple hasn't been immune to its effects, and has passed those costs onto would-be iPad customers.

While the iPad Pro packs plenty of improvements, its strongest selling point is what meets your eyes right away: the display. It also relies on a faster processor that makes a meaningful difference in intensive apps. Picking between it and the Air comes down to how you plan to take advantage of the Pro's advanced spec sheet.

The iPad Air's laminated IPS LED display is great, with solid color accuracy, P3 wide color gamut support and a pixel density of 264 ppi that makes text crisp and clear to read. The iPad Pro also has a pixel density of 264 ppi, but that's where the similarities end.

At 1,000 nits and up to 1,600 nits with HDR, the Pro's brighter tandem OLED display is miles ahead of the Air's 500-nit display. It relies on two OLED panels stacked on each other to boost brightness and color accuracy. With a contrast ratio of 2,000,000:1, it has incredibly deep blacks, which are appreciated for video creation and consumption alike.

Its 120Hz ProMotion display also feels smoother as you work through app menus, play games or simply scroll through the interface. To conserve battery, it can drop down to 10Hz while displaying images or other static content like a webpage. To reduce reflections and hide smudges, Apple also offers a nano-texture glass option at an additional cost for the top-tier Pro models.

The latest iPad Air launched in March 2026 and relies on Apple's M4 chip, while the Pro stepped up to an M5 in October 2025. To put that in context, the iPad Pro lineup used M4 back in 2024. The M4 processor is more than enough for most tasks, including gaming and video editing. It can handle rendering, media editing and on-device AI tools with no problem.

However, we found that the M5 in the iPad Pro was twice as fast when it came to running local AI models for advanced image generation tools. It offers 45 percent higher graphics performance and 15 percent faster multithreaded performance over the M4 processor.

With the M5 chip, you'll shave off a couple of seconds across intensive tasks. Admittedly, these are niche use cases, but if you want the best hardware Apple offers, paying more for the Pro model saves you time across the experience. The uptick in performance also lets the iPad Pro drive external displays at 120Hz, while the Air is restricted to 60Hz.

While the camera is seldom on the priority list when considering an iPad, the iPad Pro relies on some nifty tech uncommon among tablets. A Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) sensor next to the Pro models' rear camera helps with better autofocus and AR scanning.

Through third-party apps like Polycam, it can make floor maps of your home and develop 3D renders. Apple's Measure app lets the iPad Pro accurately measure item heights and the distance between objects, making it a great assistant when you're getting new furniture or rearranging the house. While the iPad Air also has the Measure app, it lacks this sensor that enhances its accuracy.

On the front, the Pro supports Face ID, letting you unlock your tablet without a password, while the iPad Air still relies on a fingerprint sensor for Touch ID. The advanced TrueDepth camera array also grants the ability to develop a spatial render of your face for Animoji and Memoji, or Portrait Mode selfies with background blur adjustments.

The iPad Pro comes with twice the base storage (128GB vs. 256GB), plus quad speakers compared to the Air's stereo speaker setup. It also supports fast charging with a 60W power adapter (not included), while its Thunderbolt 3 / USB 4 USB-C port can transfer large files faster and drive external monitors at 120Hz. The Pros used to have more RAM than the Air models, but the M4 Air matches them with 12GB of unified memory.

The iPad Pro keeps these advantages in a body that's only 5.3mm (0.21 inches) deep, slimmer than the already impressive 6.1mm (0.24 inches) of the iPad Air. They offer the same 10 hours of battery life for web browsing and video streaming. Individually, these features may not mean much outside of specific purposes. But together, they can make a compelling argument for the cost.

Despite these advantages, there's not enough here for a casual user that would justify spending $450 more for the iPad Pro. At $749, the iPad Air strikes the right balance of performance and features despite Apple's price hike this year from its prior price of $599. If you aren't going to take advantage of the iPad Pro's extra horsepower for video and photo editing, or by making the iPad your primary work device, your needs will be served just as well by the more affordable iPad Air.

#299. Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?

German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But how?

Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.

In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.

Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure."

The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, said it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.

Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country.

"We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot."

A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Bergeragreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation."

In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable.

Many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek. The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached.

Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic.

Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation.

"We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW.

China's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage.

Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500.

A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security."

PwC said Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China.

These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those new technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms.

"The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany.

With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit.

Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi, which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year.

"Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned.

Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well.

Domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA).

IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability.

In Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result? They have a capacity of 1.1 to 1.2 million cars and utilization of about 250,000."

Last year, those same Italian plants built just 214,000 passenger cars, according to the FIM Cisl trade union, the fewest since 1954.

For Germany, the issue isn't a lack of expertise or ambition; it's that reforms to huge industries often get weighed down by caution and red tape.

As the country's auto giants try to push through painful cuts, RWTH Aachen University's Kampker warned that if they fail to address their shortcomings, "we will see more production sites closing and a substantial shift of industrial investment and employment away from Germany."

"There is still an opportunity to reverse this trend, but the window of opportunity is narrowing," Kampker concluded.

#298. Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA says nearby phones will be jammed too.

CTIA said jamming test showed “interference… up to two and a half miles away.”

The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.

Wireless industry lobby group CTIA said a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing:

The pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts.

CTIA said the pilot test shows “that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications.”

The FCC approved the jamming order at its meeting yesterday. “Today, we are finally authorizing state and local prisons and jails to use targeted jamming against contraband cell phones for the first time,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said. “The technology has advanced to the point where it can be focused with geographic precision. No facility will be required to do it.”

The Communications Act prohibits willful or malicious interference with licensed or authorized radio communications, and the FCC has previously interpreted this to prohibit non-federal entities from using jamming technology on contraband devices at prisons. Yesterday’s vote provides an exception for state and local correctional facilities. The FCC says its jammer prohibitions do not apply to federal agencies because the federal government’s use of spectrum is not regulated by the agency.

Carr said that “contraband cell phones continue to pour into prisons by the thousands each year,” with “estimates indicat[ing] that as many as 500,000 inmates nationwide have regular access to these devices.” He said the phones have been used to plan scams, drug trafficking, and violent attacks.

“In Georgia, an incarcerated gang leader directed a drive-by shooting that killed two 13-year-old boys at a birthday party,” Carr said, referring to a 2024 shooting.

Carr defended the plan against criticism that it will block legitimate communications outside the prisons, saying it includes safeguards to prevent that.

“Those that want to use the technology will apply to the FCC, explain how they plan to deploy it, and show through testing that it stays inside the designated area and doesn’t interfere with lawful communications outside the prison walls,” Carr said. “Communities nearby will receive notice before operations start. We’re also seeking comment on next steps, including ways to close remaining loopholes on other frequencies and the possibility of quiet zones around correctional facilities.”

Freedom of the Press Foundation Chief of Advocacy Seth Stern said the FCC should have considered the benefits of contraband phones being used to document abuses inside prisons.

“Prisons are the most secretive government institutions in the country and people wishing to expose abuses and inhumane conditions from the inside often do not have many options,” Stern wrote in a letter to FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez’s office, which was included on the FCC docket. “Last year’s Oscar-nominated film, The Alabama Solution, used footage incarcerated people captured with contraband cell phones to show Americans some of the awful things that go on in state prisons that they’d have no other way of seeing. The same footage bolstered an ongoing DOJ investigation into Alabama prisons and was crucial evidence in a civil lawsuit by Steven Davis, who was brutally killed by prison guards, that eventually settled.”

Jamming contraband cellphones was supported by prison phone companies ViaPath (aka Global Tel*Link) and NCIC Correctional Services, the National District Attorneys Association, the Correctional Leaders Association, and National Association of Police Organizations.

“Inmates have used these phones to coordinate attacks against correctional officers and their families, as well as inmate violence, strikes, disturbances, and full-scale riots,” the National Association of Police Organizations said. “They also use contraband phones to organize deliveries of illegal drugs and weapons into correctional facilities. These dangers underscore the need to authorize indoor jamming in state and local correctional facilities.”

Gomez, the only Democrat on the three-member commission, said she’s concerned about potential unintended consequences, but voted with Republicans to allow jamming after safeguards were added to the order.

“For the last 90 years, the Federal Communications Commission has prohibited jamming by non-federal actors and even prohibited jamming equipment to be introduced into the American market,” Gomez said. “That is because jamming devices are specifically designed to interfere with communications devices in order to render them un-usable.”

Gomez said that “jamming can prevent devices from completing 911 and emergency calls as well as interfere with communications networks used by fire, police, Emergency Medical Services, and other public safety entities.” She also said making jamming equipment available in the American market could lead to “unauthorized sale of this hazardous equipment,” and that “the accessibility of jamming equipment can itself motivate criminal enterprise.” Criminals have used “Wi-Fi jammers to disrupt security systems, security cameras, and cellphones to conduct robberies at homes and at stores,” she said.

Gomez said she’s glad the final order includes safeguards “to ensure that jamming is contained to this unique use, to permit jamming by a very limited category of authorized actors, and to take as much care as possible to prevent jamming and jamming equipment from becoming a hazard to safety.”

Gomez partially dissented because she is worried the FCC will let correctional facilities and prison phone companies charge higher prices for inmate calling services that connect inmates with family members. Under US law, the FCC sets limits on those prices and considers prisons’ and jails’ safety and security costs when deciding how much money they can charge, she said.

Gomez said, “While correctional facilities should have safety and security services like jamming to prevent criminal activity, it is not the responsibility of the families of incarcerated people to pay for the costs of these measures… Jamming is specifically designed to block communications and is certainly not necessary to provide phone and video calls for incarcerated individuals. We should have made this clear in today’s order. Because we failed to do so, I dissent in part.”

The FCC order could be challenged in court. The CTIA has argued that the FCC “has no authority to allow jamming” under the Communications Act, which directs the FCC to prevent interference.

AT&T said the FCC’s legal justification “is premised on a fundamental factual error: the assumption that jammers will only block ‘unauthorized’ communications without impacting lawful uses. There is no way to jam some communications on a spectrum band but not others. That is because radio jammers ‘block all wireless communications on affected spectrum bands,’ and, as the FCC has noted in the past, ‘cannot differentiate between contraband devices and legitimate devices.’”

AT&T said that “there is simply no way to limit the reach of jammers to the confines of a given facility. Jammers have been shown to cause interference outside the facilities in which they operate, greatly increasing the risk that someone living or traveling nearby will be impacted.”

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#296. Why does your phone say no service even with a SIM card?

If your calls and texts aren't going through, try these recommendations.

The modern electronic device has made a lot of strides in ensuring that it lets you know when something has gone awry. Things like computers, game consoles and tablets will often find a way to alert you to an issue, which makes it easier to troubleshoot any potential problems that may arise.

On your phone, you may notice one of these alerts in the form of a notification that says, "No SIM card installed." This can be alarming, as it's possible that you may not know what a SIM card even does. Or if you do know what the SIM card does, it can lead to some worrying conclusions as you try to troubleshoot it.

Fixing a SIM card error is a task that requires some diagnostic detective work, or if you're extra unlucky, some actual physical work. Thankfully, there are a lot of tools, both in your phone's settings and in the real world, that can assist with a potential fix.

When a SIM card error leaves you without service, the phone will still work and power on; it will just be without its main features. The only thing that needs to be done is to take it out and put it right back in. This is usually caused by dropping the phone or ithe card not being properly seated when it was serviced for you, but you can use a SIM ejector tool to take it out. If you don't have one, something as simple as a paper clip or safety pin will usually do the trick.

It's always worth finding out if it's something as simple as a carrier outage, which is entirely possible. If you have access to another device on a different carrier and it can connect to the internet or make a phone call, that could indicate a network outage specific to your carrier. Asking a local friend or family member using the same service whether their phone is working properly can confirm a carrier outage or eliminate it as a possibility.

Your phone may be using an eSIM card, which replaces the physical card with a digital SIM. These are great, but they tend to have unique issues with international travel. If you're using an eSIM card, the way you access settings on an iPhone is slightly different from Android. On an iPhone, eSIM cards are located in Cellular or Mobile Data in the Settings menu, while Android stores them in a setting called SIM Manager. By turning on data roaming, you may fix any sort of problems you're having.

A SIM card or "no service" error can sometimes be something at a software level as opposed to something being wrong with the card. One of the more common fixes is simply toggling airplane mode on and off. Airplane mode can be found by swiping down from the top of your phone and tapping the airplane button.

You may also be able to do a quick network reset, which sounds bad but has zero effect on your personal files. Doing a network reset on an iPhone is largely similar to the process on Android. It should be noted, however, that the iPhone's network reset is in the Transfer or Reset section of Settings, while Android stores it in Reset Options, also in Settings. You will need to sign back into your Wi-Fi, however, along with some other connections.

We all get busy in life, and if you haven't paid your bill, then your SIM card will simply stop connecting to your carrier's network. It may seem like a simple thing, but sometimes the simple solutions are blindingly obvious. If you pay your bill online, check your account to see if you've missed a payment or if your service hasn't been suspended for some other reason.

Getting no service on your phone may not even have anything to do with a bad SIM card or an inactive account. You may just be in a place with limited to no service available, or a cellphone tower may be blocked by something. Move around and look for someplace that you actually can connect, as the error may be a result of poor service in that area.
